observed_evidence.note: Serial synthesis was introduced deliberately to fix an ordering bug — a short later sentence could overtake a long earlier one. The docstring claims it costs no latency because 'chunk N+1 synthesizes while chunk N plays'. That gives only ONE chunk of lookahead, so any call slower than the chunk currently playing becomes audible silence. Ordering is a property of the index, not of serialising.

sample_text: Root cause found. Somadian silently truncates every reply at two thousand characters. The cut landed inside a bold marker, orphaning it. There is no error, no counter, and no log line. The bottleneck underneath it is that playback is far slower than generation. I cannot measure it yet, because health gives queue depths but no durations.

current.label: Uniform sentence chunks (shipped)
pros: Fastest possible first word — chunk 1 is one short sentence.
Chunk boundaries land on sentence ends, so prosody and intonation stay natural.
A failed chunk costs one sentence. At ~3% edge-tts failure that is a small, survivable hole.
Barge-in feels instant: an interruption takes effect within one short chunk.
Already shipped, simple, and predictable — no tuning constants to get wrong.
cons: Pays the fixed per-chunk synthesis overhead N times for N sentences — worst throughput of any strategy.
Never builds a playback buffer, so there is no slack to absorb one slow chunk.
In the high-overhead regime, stalls compound and the pipeline never catches up.
More chunks means more network round trips, so more chances to hit the ~3% failure.

proposed.label: Ramped chunks, buffer-targeted
pros: Keeps the fast first word — chunk 1 stays small by design.
Amortises the fixed overhead across far fewer, larger chunks.
Builds a buffer, so one slow synthesis or network hiccup is absorbed instead of heard.
Fewer round trips — fewer opportunities for the edge-tts failure.
Closed-loop on buffer depth, it self-regulates under machine load instead of falling behind permanently.
cons: 🔴 Blast radius grows: a failed chunk now loses a whole paragraph rather than one sentence.
🔴 Barge-in gets worse — interrupting cannot take effect until the current chunk ends, or must kill playback mid-paragraph. For a voice you talk over, this is a real regression.
Large chunks may hit TTS length limits or degrade prosody; unknown until measured.
Adds tuning constants — and with the wrong ones it is strictly worse than uniform.
Only helps at all in the high-overhead regime. At 1200ms it changes nothing.

parallel.label: Parallel synthesis, uniform chunks (measured winner)
pros: **Zero stalls measured** — playback never starved once, versus 4 stalls serial.
Keeps small sentence chunks, so it retains every advantage of the shipped strategy: instant barge-in, natural prosody, and a one-sentence blast radius when a synthesis fails.
First word unchanged (1718ms vs 3386ms serial — in fact faster here).
Attacks the actual dominant term: spends roughly the **max** of the latency distribution instead of the **sum**.
One tuning knob (worker count), and it is not sensitive — all 5 chunks finished by 3.3s against 29.6s of playback.
Fixes the cause rather than hiding it; ramping only buys more time to absorb the same stall.
cons: 🔴 Re-opens the ordering hazard that serialisation was introduced to fix. Order must come from the slot index, and a regression there returns a bug that is confusing and intermittent.
N concurrent cloud calls burst edge-tts; **rate limits untested** — a long reply could fan out to dozens of simultaneous requests.
OpenVoice clone runs per chunk; thread-safety and GPU/model-lock contention **not verified** beyond ×4.
Work is wasted on barge-in — chunks synthesized ahead are discarded if the user interrupts.
More temp audio files in flight; unbounded fan-out on a very long reply needs a cap.

scenarios.label: Serial synthesis, uniform sentence chunks
scenarios.note: One synthesis worker. Chunk N+1 only begins once chunk N finishes, so the pipeline spends the SUM of a highly variable distribution and stalls whenever one call runs long.
